sections.heading: What are Graph BFS & DFS?
sections.content: A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. BFS (Breadth-First Search) explores it in waves: all neighbors first, then neighbors of neighbors, using a queue. DFS (Depth-First Search) follows one path as deep as it can before backing up, using recursion or a stack. Unlike a tree, a graph can contain cycles, so you must keep a visited set to avoid looping forever. Both run in O(V + E), where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Explore everything reachable from a starting node
Count connected components, islands or provinces
Find the shortest path in an unweighted graph or grid (BFS)
Check if a path exists between two nodes
Detect cycles, check bipartiteness or validate a tree
Flood fill, matrix traversal and region problems
Search an implicit graph where states are nodes (word ladder, lock combinations)
Keywords: connected, reachable, islands, shortest path, minimum steps, nearest, clone, bipartite, cycle

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: BFS is a ripple spreading from a stone dropped in water: it reaches everything at distance 1 before anything at distance 2, which is why it finds shortest paths. DFS is exploring a maze by always taking the next corridor until you hit a dead end, then retracing your steps. In both cases the visited set is your breadcrumb trail so you never walk the same corridor twice.

Visited Set Rules
items: BFS: mark a node visited when you ADD it to the queue, so it is never queued twice
Recursive DFS: mark a node visited when you ENTER it
Iterative DFS: mark when you POP it (or when you push, if you only need reachability)
For grids you can mark visited in place (overwrite the cell), but only if modifying the input is allowed
Loop over all start nodes when the graph can be disconnected

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting the visited set, which causes infinite loops on graphs with cycles
Marking visited when popping from the BFS queue, which lets nodes be queued many times
Starting the search from only one node when the graph can be disconnected
Adding edges in only one direction for an undirected graph
Using the parent trick for cycle detection in a directed graph (use 3 states instead)
Skipping bounds checks on grids, or mixing up row and column order
Running a BFS from each source separately instead of one multi-source BFS
Recursive DFS on a graph with 100,000+ nodes, which can overflow the stack
Modifying the input grid when the problem requires it to stay unchanged

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: BFS uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, while DFS uses recursion or a stack and explores deeply
Always keep a visited set, and mark nodes when you enqueue them in BFS
Loop over every node as a start to handle disconnected graphs and count components
Grids are implicit graphs: use a directions array and bounds checks
Multi-source BFS starts from all sources at once for nearest-distance problems
Both run in O(V + E), which is O(rows * cols) on a grid
